claims.text: Approximately 70% cold rolling followed immediately by rapid single-step annealing is the proposed intervention for HfZrTiTa0.53.
The proposed treatment will induce a heterogeneous or bimodal grain-size distribution in HfZrTiTa0.53.
The proposed treatment may form nanometric ductile precipitates at grain boundaries in HfZrTiTa0.53.
Fine grains in the heterogeneous microstructure will help retain high strength.
Coarser grains and/or ductile precipitates will increase strain hardening and ductility.
Microstructural heterogeneity will delay tensile necking by sustaining plastic flow.
The mixed grain sizes and ductile precipitates will distribute local stresses more uniformly.
Annealing in the 600–800 °C range is likely to be suitable for creating the targeted microstructure in HfZrTiTa0.53.
The treatment will increase uniform tensile elongation from approximately 13.5% to at least 20%.
The treatment will preserve a yield strength of approximately 786 MPa.
The treatment will preserve a compressive strength of approximately 1314 MPa.
The treatment will cause no reduction in impact-triggered chemical-energy release.
The initial HfZrTiTa0.53 material is a homogeneous as-cast alloy.
As-cast HfZrTiTa0.53 has a yield strength of approximately 786 MPa.
As-cast HfZrTiTa0.53 has a compressive strength of approximately 1314 MPa.
The reported 13.5% terminal strain is a baseline uniform tensile elongation for HfZrTiTa0.53.
HfZrTiTa0.53 has proven impact-triggered chemical-energy release.
The predicted ductility benefit applies at room and moderately elevated temperatures under quasi-static tensile loading near 10^-3 s^-1.
Matched tension, compression, and high-strain-rate impact tests against an as-cast control can test the hypothesis.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant tensile-elongation increase, or any reduction in yield strength, compressive strength, or impact-energy release, will falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis treats the reported 13.5% terminal strain as though it were uniform tensile elongation. Terminal strain and uniform tensile elongation are distinct metrics, so the baseline for the claimed improvement is internally inconsistent.
The boundary permits no significant degradation in compression or energetic response, whereas the falsification rule treats any reduction as falsifying; these impose different tolerances.
